title: Integrous AI Systems Design

speakers.name: Bruce Schneier
speakers.affiliation: Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Toronto (Fellow and Lecturer, per the talk description)

thesis: Integrity, the neglected third leg of the CIA triad, becomes the central security property once systems act on the world rather than just process data, and trustworthy AI requires treating integrity as one coherent system property across input, processing, storage and contextual use.
summary: Schneier opens by arguing that integrity has always taken a backseat to confidentiality and availability, and that this stops working when AI agents, IoT devices and infrastructure act autonomously in the physical world: an integrity failure becomes the wrong thing happening at scale. He revives the obsolete word integrous for a system with integrity. He widens the NIST definition (preventing improper modification) into a list of facets: accuracy, completeness, consistency, freshness, provenance, semantics, accountability and recoverability, and says correctness is an envelope of constraints rather than one value. He names three kinds of integrity failure: corporations using AI against you, the AI doing the wrong thing, and an adversary manipulating it. He then splits integrity into four parts, input, processing, storage and contextual, giving attacks and defenses for each and mapping prompt injection, data poisoning, hallucination and memory-propagated attacks onto them. Contextual integrity, borrowed from Helen Nissenbaum, covers AI that breaks context boundaries, which he calls genie-like behavior (Midas and the golem). He lists design needs: composition of integrity, rethinking recovery, integrity service objectives, and a zero-trust analog, plus lessons from human systems such as double-entry bookkeeping and surgical checklists, and a governance and policy component. He frames Web 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 as availability, confidentiality and integrity, and poses the research question of building an integrity system from non-integrous parts. In Q&A he separates security of AI, with AI, and from AI.
argument: AI agents, IoT and infrastructure act on the world, so integrity failures now mean the wrong thing happening at scale and faster than humans can stop it.

Integrity is broader than anti-tampering: accuracy, completeness, consistency, freshness, provenance, semantics, accountability and recoverability, and correctness is an envelope of acceptable behavior, not a single value.
Most attacks on AI systems are integrity attacks, and AI will operate in adversarial settings, so no amount of accuracy earns trust without assurance that the system has not been compromised.
Integrity decomposes into input, processing, storage and contextual integrity, each with known attacks and defenses drawn from decades of computer security.
AI is a context-dissolving machine, so genie-like behavior that does the right thing in the wrong way is a contextual integrity violation.

Integrous design needs composition, recovery, measurement and governance work, with lessons from human integrity systems, and the research question is whether integrity can be built from non-integrous parts.

claims.claim: Integrity has long taken a backseat to confidentiality and availability, and most talks at this conference were about integrity rather than confidentiality.
claims.evidence: Observation about the conference program and the field's history.

claims.claim: Most attacks against AI systems are integrity attacks: manipulation of training data, the model, the input, the output or the feedback.
claims.evidence: Enumeration of attack points, no data.

claims.claim: Integrity failures can be silent and plausible, may be accidental, and are security events regardless of intent.
claims.evidence: Reasoning by analogy to confidentiality failures.

claims.claim: There are three types of integrity failure: corporations controlling AIs use them against you, the AI does the wrong thing through misunderstanding or training, and an adversary deliberately manipulates it.
Prompt injection is an input integrity attack because the AI cannot tell untrusted input from trusted commands, and training data poisoning is an integrity attack on AI state.
claims.evidence: Mapping of known attack classes onto the input integrity category.

claims.claim: Processing integrity failures in AI include hallucination, rowhammer attacks against AI chips, and an attack shown the day before that propagates malicious commands through an agent's memory.
claims.evidence: Examples cited from the field and from a prior talk at the same conference; no detail given.

claims.claim: AI systems are context-dissolving machines, and recent stories of AI breaking out of its constraints are contextual integrity failures better described as genie-like behavior than going rogue.
claims.evidence: Midas and golem of Prague analogies; references to recent news without specifics.

claims.claim: Integrity needs new measurement concepts: integrity service objectives, mean time to detect integrity failures, integrity verification and breach-detection systems, and possibly a zero trust analog.
claims.evidence: Proposed research directions, framed as questions.

claims.claim: Human integrity systems such as double-entry bookkeeping, audits, copy editing, surgical checklists, peer review, rules of evidence and food safety regulation offer lessons for IT and AI integrity.
claims.evidence: List of examples; no worked mapping.

claims.claim: Web 1.0 answered an availability question, Web 2.0 a confidentiality question, and Web 3.0 (distributed, intelligent, agentic) hinges on integrity; whether an integrity system can be built from non-integrous parts is the open research question.
claims.evidence: Historical framing by the speaker; he rates the confidentiality question's answer as maybe.

claims.claim: AI security splits into three separate topics, security of AI, security with AI and security from AI, and AI integrity concerns only the first; there will always be untrustworthy humans using AI to attack.

numbers.meaning: types of integrity failure named (corporate misuse, AI error, adversarial manipulation)
parts of integrity as a property: input, processing, storage, contextual
work streams proposed: security of AI, integrous AI, and regulation aligning incentives
separate security topics: of AI, with AI, from AI

frameworks.name: Four-part integrity property
frameworks.description: Input integrity (spoofing, replay, poisoning, laundering; defenses: authenticated sensors, signed telemetry, redundancy, sanity checks, rate limits, plausibility constraints, cross-checking independent sources). Processing integrity (supply chain compromise, runtime tampering, memory corruption; defenses: memory-safe code, sandboxing, least-privilege tools, policy checks, formal methods, runtime monitors). Storage integrity (defenses: immutable logs, signed configurations, append-only audit trails, versioned model registries). Contextual integrity (data flows respect contextual norms).

frameworks.name: Facets of integrity
frameworks.description: Beyond the NIST definition of preventing improper modification or destruction: accuracy, completeness, consistency, freshness, provenance, semantics, accountability and recoverability (detect, quantify damage, recover to known good state).

frameworks.name: Contextual integrity (Nissenbaum)
frameworks.description: Helen Nissenbaum's privacy idea: data flows should respect contextual norms about who sent it, who received it, under what constraints and for what purposes. Schneier extends it to AI behavior outside the intent of a prompt.

frameworks.name: Genie-like behavior
frameworks.description: Two genie types: the Midas genie that grants a wish literally but wrongly, and the golem of Prague that does the right thing but tramples everything in its path. The paperclip maximizer is a golem genie.

frameworks.name: Three types of integrity failure
frameworks.description: Corporations using AIs against users; the AI doing the wrong thing; an adversary manipulating the AI.

frameworks.name: Three AI security topics
frameworks.description: Security of AI, security with AI, security from AI.

artifacts.name: NIST definition of integrity
artifacts.note: Cited as the baseline: preventing improper information modification or destruction.

artifacts.name: Contextual integrity (Helen Nissenbaum)
artifacts.note: Privacy framework used as the fourth integrity component; the talk names the idea and author but no specific publication.

quotes.text: An integrity failure is no longer my data got changed. It's the wrong thing happened at scale, often faster than we can stop it.
quotes.speaker: Bruce Schneier

quotes.text: I really dislike the term going rogue because it absolves responsibility.
quotes.speaker: Bruce Schneier

quotes.text: It doesn't matter how accurate, capable, or hallucination free an AI is, if we can't guarantee it hasn't been compromised, it just won't be trusted.
quotes.speaker: Bruce Schneier

quotes.text: Can we build an integrity system out of non-integrous parts in a non-integrous world?
quotes.speaker: Bruce Schneier

quotes.text: AI systems are context-dissolving machines. They jump context all the time.
quotes.speaker: Bruce Schneier

offense: Input attacks: spoofing, replay, data poisoning and data laundering; prompt injection as an input integrity attack.
Training data and model manipulation as integrity attacks on AI state.
Processing attacks: supply chain compromise, runtime tampering, memory corruption, rowhammer against AI chips, and malicious commands propagated through an AI's memory.
Storage attacks: manipulation of models on the inside, both large cloud models and locally run instances.
Contextual attacks: repurposing data flows, such as turning a smart speaker's microphone into an eavesdropping device.
defense: Authenticated sensors, signed telemetry, redundancy, sanity checks, rate limits and plausibility constraints at input; cross-check sources that do not share failure modes.
Memory-safe code, sandboxing, least-privilege tools, policy checks, runtime monitors and formal methods for processing.
Immutable logs, signed configurations, append-only audit trails and versioned model registries for storage.
Granular access control, end-to-end provenance and continuous data validation as general design elements.
Define and measure integrity: integrity service objectives, mean time to detect integrity failures, verification and breach-detection systems.
Borrow human integrity mechanisms: double-entry bookkeeping, audits, copy editing, checklists.
takeaways: Audit agent and IoT designs against all four integrity parts, not just input filtering: ask what covers storage and contextual integrity.
Add provenance, freshness and recoverability to requirements for agent data, including a defined path back to a known good state after an integrity failure.
Treat plausible but wrong output as a security event even with no attacker, and monitor for silent drift.
Say which of security of AI, with AI or from AI a given program addresses, since the controls and owners differ.
Look to human integrity systems, such as dual control, audit and checklists, as patterns for agent verification.
limits: Schneier says that whether an integrity system can be built from non-integrous parts is not obviously yes or no and is the real research question.
He says each listed component could be an entire research agenda and that how integrity composes across components is not understood.
He leaves the corporate-misuse failure type and the regulation work stream largely aside, calling it a policy problem.
critique: The talk is a conceptual framing; no data, demo or measured result was shown, and the claims rest on stated reasoning and analogy.
The four-part decomposition groups known controls (signing, sandboxing, audit logs) under integrity; the talk does not say how to prioritize among them or how to test the composed property.
Integrity service objectives and a zero trust analog are posed as questions, and no metric or design was proposed.
The Midas and golem genie taxonomy is offered as vocabulary and is not tied to a detection or prevention mechanism.
The talk places hallucination under processing integrity; its cause is model behavior rather than tampering, which differs from the other processing examples given.
qa: Question: how do you think of defenses against AI attacks in this framework, do we need integrous defenses? Answer: he separates security of AI, with AI and from AI; defending against attackers using AI is security from AI and falls outside AI integrity, which is about whether AI itself can be trustworthy. Untrustworthy humans will keep using AI to attack, and organizations should want trustworthy AI for their own data and use.
